I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event

Negative Appraisals.value: The event happened because of the way I acted
I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened

vignette: Samantha, a 25-year-old South Eastern Asian woman and married database administrator, has been struggling with intense distress following a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. The trauma of the accident has left deep psychological scars that have affected nearly every aspect of her daily life. On the day of the accident, Samantha was driving home from work when a truck, swerving to avoid an obstacle, collided head-on into her car. She vividly recalls the blaring horn of the approaching vehicle and the jarring impact that shattered the windshield and sent shards flying in all directions. The chaos and fear during those moments have left lasting triggers that continue to haunt her. Samantha reports that hearing names related to cars or traffic, engaging in arguments, or facing any kind of uncertainty triggers intense flashbacks and anxiety. These triggers are potent reminders of the accident's overwhelming helplessness and terror. For instance, a recent disagreement with her husband over minor details sent her into a panic, reliving the chaotic moments leading up to the collision. To cope with these intrusive memories and heightened states of arousal, Samantha has adopted several maladaptive strategies. She avoids situations that put physical stress on her body, such as exercise or even routine daily activities like climbing stairs. This avoidance has led her to isolate herself from friends and social gatherings, where she might encounter similar stressors. Additionally, when the memories become too overwhelming, she resorts to self-harm as a way to distract herself from the traumatic event. Samantha's negative appraisals have deepened over time, forming a cycle of distress that is difficult to break. She believes that the accident happened because of her actions and feels an intense sense of guilt for not doing more to prevent it. These self-blaming thoughts often lead her to mistrust others, feeling that they cannot understand or empathize with her experience. For example, after an argument with a coworker about database updates, Samantha was overwhelmed by the memory of the accident's chaos and felt betrayed, reinforcing her belief that people can't be trusted. This led her to further isolate herself from colleagues and social activities, exacerbating her sense of guilt and mistrust. The negative appraisals also fuel her maladaptive strategies. Her persistent self-blame and feelings of inaction guilt have made her increasingly reliant on avoidance behaviors as a means of coping. When she avoids situations that put physical stress on her body or encounters uncertainty at work, it temporarily alleviates some of the overwhelming anxiety but reinforces her negative beliefs about herself. Samantha's maladaptive strategies, while offering temporary relief, also exacerbate her triggers and negative appraisals. Her self-harm distracts her momentarily from the traumatic memories, but it leaves her feeling more isolated and guilty, reinforcing her belief that she is not doing enough to prevent such events in the future. The cumulative effect of these behaviors has significantly impacted Samantha's daily life. At work, she has become increasingly withdrawn and hesitant to engage in collaborative projects or even casual conversations with colleagues. This avoidance has led to a decline in her job performance and strained relationships at work. What finally brought Samantha to seek help was a growing realization that her isolation and maladaptive coping mechanisms were taking an immense toll on both her personal and professional life. She is most afraid of the cycle continuing indefinitely, leaving her unable to live a full and meaningful life. Yet, she is also hopeful that with support, she can break free from these patterns and regain control over her thoughts and actions. Samantha's journey towards recovery starts with understanding the intricate web of triggers, maladaptive strategies, and negative appraisals that have ensnared her. By addressing these components systematically, she hopes to rebuild trust in herself and others and find a path forward where she can live without constant fear and self-blame.
